Zimbabwe burns

By: Ntokozo Miya | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Tonight on Carte Blanche we recall the events of the Zimbabwean shutdown and explore why South Africa should be worried.

Unique Selling Point:
The story is still developing and is topical, and the insert will paint of picture of what's to come for Zimbabwe and South Africa.

Summary:
After Pres. Emmerson Mnangagwa increased the price of fuel in Zimbabwe by 150% to R45 per liter last week, the civil organisations mobilised citizens to embark on a national shutdown starting Monday 14 January.
The protesters demand: 1> an end to the economic crisis, 2> reversal of fuel increase and 3> payment of salaries in US dollars.
In reaction to the shutdown, the Zim government shut down internet and social media services in what has been called an apparent attempt to keep the rest of the world in the dark about the situation in the country.
We speak to key individuals about the impact the Zimbabwean situation will have on South Africa including a businessman who trades between the two countries and a Zimbabwean journalist who covered the events. We focus on why SA should be concerned and discuss that in detail with the Democratic Alliance who have threatened to take the matter up with ICC if Ramaphosa does not intervene to stop the human rights violations in Zim.

Further information:
Before the national shutdown, Zimbabwean civil servants rejected a 10% salary increase and planned to go on a strike in two weeks time. The strike will see 300 000 public workers take to the streets.
The fuel price increase further aggravated workers and the rest of the country, which led to the shutdown before the planned strike.
Human rights organisations have called for a stop to the human rights violations allegedly perpetrated by military police against civilians.
The SA finance department has since said that it declined to give Zimbabwe a $1billion loan.

Press Release:


Zim Shuts Down
A mere seven months after promising to put Zimbabwe on a new path to growth and prosperity, President Emmerson Mnangagwa has dealt citizens a shocking blow by raising the fuel price by 150% and standing by while his state security minister shuts down the country’s internet – a move that the country’s highest court has ruled illegal. Inflation has spiked to the highest levels ever and a vicious security services clampdown has left a dozen people dead. Carte Blanche asks how Zimbabwe could be pulled back from the brink.
Producer: Ntokozo Miya
Presenter: Derek Watts



Script:


ZIMBABWE BURNS – FINAL SCRIPT AND PROMOS

FOCUS – In the aftermath of the Zimbabwean national shutdown protests, we explore why South Africa should concern itself with the situation in the neighbouring country. [focussing on human rights violations, impact of situation on immigration and trade between the two countries]

TEASER - 01:03:45:08 – A huge hike in the fuel price led to protests, shootings and deaths, and a complete shutdown in Zimbabwe. How concerned should South Africans be about the turbulence and violence to our north?

ZANU PF YouTube Video – 2018 election campaign
Emmerson Mnangagwa
00.00 - It is time for a new Zimbabwe. It is time for hope and peace.
00:49 – Let me continue to lead into a new prosperous Zimbabwe

LINK - 00:14:16:15 – This was President Emmerson Mnangagwa's promise to the people of Zimbabwe before the elections in July last year. Now seven months into his presidency, Zimbabweans say they are yet to celebrate any kind of prosperity.

VO – In mid-January, before embarking on a European tour to attract investors to Zimbabwe, President Mnangagwa announced a petrol price hike that he said was a “corrective measure” for “increased fuel usage” and “illegal fuel trading activities.” A litre of fuel shot from R19 to around R45.

Lovejoy Mutongwiza – Zimbabwean journalist
01:07:19:16 – As if that was not enough, the following day, government tabled a 10% increase, salary increase to civil servants which was considered to be a mockery by many because they thought if government can increase fuel prices by 150%, why would they then go on and increase salaries by 10%.

VO – While two South African reporters were barred from reporting on the protests that followed, and were even deported, Zimbabwean journalist Lovejoy Mutongwiza was at the centre of the action. The shutdown was meant to be peaceful, but was apparently hijacked by “rogue elements”.

Lovejoy Mutongwiza – Zimbabwean journalist – Clip MVI_1262
00:50 – ... People were blocking commuters from getting into the CBD, blocking vehicles from getting into the CBD so that workers would not be able to get to work.
01:12 – People were now actually engaging in fist fights with the police. Some were confiscating police guns. Some were even taking away army guns.

VO – And that was just on day one of the protests..

LINK - 01:01:01:08 – On the second day of protests, the minister of state for security ordered service providers to shut down the internet.

VO – A Zimbabwean high court later ruled that state security minister Owen Ncube was not authorised to make that call, and ordered that internet services be restored.
With the eyes of social media closed, it was a free for all, says Mutongwiza.

Lovejoy Mutongwiza – Zimbabwean journalist – Clip MVI_1263
02:02 – Looting was mainly done in Bulawayo, that's where most shops were looted. And we also started receiving reports that soldiers had been deployed in Harare.
02:23 – There were gunshots which were being fired around about 11 in the morning.
02:38 – That's when all reports of violence, from everywhere, be it Harare, Gweru, Tare, everywhere, It was just chaotic.

VO – As South Africa heads to the polls later this year, immigration is on top of the agenda for many local political parties.
It's unclear how many Zimbabweans live in South Africa because many of them are undocumented. Estimates range from two to five million.
The DA says the Zimbabwean crisis will spill over our borders if it is ignored.
The party's Stevens Mokgalapa, condemned the use of excessive force, as well as the subsequent internet blackout.

Derek - 00:54:18:22 – Why do you think there was this communication blackout?

Stevens Mokgalapa – DA MP
00:36:35:10 – … It is to allow this kleptocratic regime of Mnangagwa to go and act with impunity and do a lot of civil damage, and to round up civil activists.

VO – The DA says President Cyril Ramaphosa must intervene, and threatens to go to the UN security council if he doesn't act.

Derek - 00:54:41:00 – Is it reasonable to expect our president to intervene and resolve issues in another country?

Stevens Mokgalapa – DA MP
00:38:51:05 – Of course, of course.
00:47:00:16 – We have to make sure that we fix the problem where the problem is - at the source, not at the recipient. We are a receiving state of the problems of Zimbabwe but we have got to solve the problem there, both politically, economically to ensure that there is stability in Zimbabwe.

VO – Mokgalapa denies that the DA wants to restrict immigrant traffic into South Africa.

Stevens Mokgalapa – DA MP
00:48:18:16 – ... Any country should be able to manage its borders, should be able to document the people that come in through its borders. ... So it's not a question of restriction of movement, it's a question of management and control of movement of people.

VO – The DA and the EFF are on the same page as far as Zimbabwe is concerned.

Julius Malema – EFF Leader
00:04 – South Africa must contribute towards the bailout of Zimbabwe.
00:16 – If you don't help Zimbabweans, the border is going to be flooded by them.
00:27 – You are always complaining: hey, there are Zimbabweans here! The only way not to have them is by helping them in their own country.

VO – Julius Malema says the focus should be on developing the country in economic ruin.

Julius Malema – EFF Leader
00:44 – We must give a conditional grant to the Zimbabweans and it must be a grant dedicated to developmental programs which will help Zimbabwe to stand on its own.

VO – Ramaphosa said his government was consulting with Zimbabwe and called on the world to lift economic sanctions against Zimbabwe.
In an earlier statement, the department of international relations and cooperation wrote that it was “confident that the measures being taken by the Zimbabwean government will resolve the situation.”

LINK - 01:04:21:20 – The R45 a liter fuel hike has made life even more challenging for most Zimbabweans, and also for businesspeople who trade between the two countries.

VO – The cost of living has escalated beyond the means of ordinary Zimbabweans, says Ngqabutho Mabhena, of the African Diaspora Forum, an organisation that supports immigrants in South Africa.

Ngqabutho Mabhena – African Diaspora Forum
00:22:53:15 – Prices will certainly shoot up. For instance, last week, your public transport which used to cost 50 cents has gone up to about $2.50, some charging $3.

VO – While some Zimbabweans are desperately trying to adapt to rising costs, many are anxious about safety in the wake of the apparent security crackdown.

Ngqabutho Mabhena – African Diaspora Forum
00:19:11:12 – When people's security is threatened, it is then that people will start to say: let me maybe skip the country.
00:24:30:20 – ... It really means that you will have more people coming into South Africa to impart on the social services of South Africa.

VO – Shortly before the Zim elections in July last year, President Mnangagwa told Carte Blanche he was committed to making things easier for businesspeople.

2018 Carte Blanche interview
Emmerson Mnangagwa
6th bite - We must create an environment: the ease of doing business, the cost of doing business. We look at how those things can be done.

VO – Mnangagwa has done nothing of the sort, says trader Denis Juru.

Denis Juru – Cross Border Traders Association
00:01:45:13 – People are definitely suffering because there is no employment. This is the only way of living - buying goods from outside the country and you sell to other people and then you buy also from other people what they sell that you don't have.
00:02:54:00 – … with the fuel hike, now it means transporting goods to Zimbabwe is a bit expensive.

Derek - 00:12:35:15 - What about the rebate promised by the president?

Denis Juru – Cross Border Traders Association
00:06:19:21 – ... it is very, very difficult to apply for it. Most of these informal traders are not registered. That rebate is for registered people and to be registered needs a lot of money so most of the traders are not registered.

VO – Juru warns that if informal trade between the two countries collapses, even more Zimbabweans will look to South Africa for relief.

Denis Juru – Cross Border Traders Association
00:02:11:18 – People are coming in to South Africa, they are coming in to Botswana and Zambia as well.
00:02:41:06 – I think that's when we experience xenophobia because the influx is very, very high.

VO – Carte Blanche emailed the Zimbabwean presidential office as well as the ruling party to request comment from President Mnangagwa. As yet, we have not received a response.
Earlier this week, Mnangagwa cut his international trip short to return to Zimbabwe. He promised to investigate reports of violence, but said nothing about a review of the fuel price at the heart of the protests.

LINK - 00:14:36:21 – Zimbabweans pledge to pound on the government's door till their demands for jobs, higher salaries and lower fuel prices are met.

Lovejoy Mutongwiza – Zimbabwean journalist – Clip MVI_1266
00:41 – Despite these pressure groups and civil society groups having called for another shutdown, I don't think they are going to engage in another shutdown, especially judging by how people were beaten the last time out. Those visuals, those memories are still fresh.

VO - It remains to be seen if the man known for proclaiming that “the voice of the people is the voice of God” will hear the cries of his people, and come up with a bold new plan for Zimbabwe.


ZIM PROMOS

PROMO 1 - 10sec
VO - Just how concerned should South Africans be about the turbulence and violence to our north? Politicians say if President Ramaphosa doesn't intervene, we'll feel the pressure at our borders.

PROMO 2 – 15sec
VO - Following the recent turmoil in the neighbouring country, politicians say South Africa must urgently intervene in Zimbabwe or face an immigration crisis.

Julius Malema – EFF Leader
00:16 – If you don't help Zimbabweans, the border is going to be flooded by them.

PROMO 3 – 15sec
VO - The impact of the recent shutdown in Zimbabwe will be felt across the border in SA, so say politicians and civil organisations.

Ngqabutho Mabhena – African Diaspora Forum
00:19:11:12 – When people's security is threatened, it is then that people will start to say: let me maybe skip the country.

Julius Malema – EFF Leader
00:16 – If you don't help Zimbabweans, the border is going to be flooded by them.

PROMO 4 – 30sec
VO - A huge hike in the fuel price led to protests, shootings and deaths, and a complete shutdown in Zimbabwe.

Lovejoy Mutongwiza – Zimbabwean journalist – Clip MVI_1262
01:12 – People were now actually engaging in fist fights with the police. Some were confiscating police guns. Some were even taking away army guns.

VO - But why exactly should South Africa concern itself with the goings-on next-door?

Julius Malema – EFF Leader
00:16 – If you don't help Zimbabweans, the border is going to be flooded by them.

Stevens Mokgalapa – DA MP
00:47:00:16 – ... We are a receiving state of the problems of Zimbabwe.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Tonight on Carte Blanche we recall the events of the Zimbabwean shutdown and explore why South Africa should be worried.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: The story is still developing and is topical, and the insert will paint of picture of what's to come for Zimbabwe and South Africa.
metadata.Summary: After Pres. Emmerson Mnangagwa increased the price of fuel in Zimbabwe by 150% to R45 per liter last week, the civil organisations mobilised citizens to embark on a national shutdown starting Monday 14 January. The protesters demand: 1> an end to the economic crisis, 2> reversal of fuel increase and 3> payment of salaries in US dollars. In reaction to the shutdown, the Zim government shut down internet and social media services in what has been called an apparent attempt to keep the rest of the world in the dark about the situation in the country. We speak to key individuals about the impact the Zimbabwean situation will have on South Africa including a businessman who trades between the two countries and a Zimbabwean journalist who covered the events. We focus on why SA should be concerned and discuss that in detail with the Democratic Alliance who have threatened to take the matter up with ICC if Ramaphosa does not intervene to stop the human rights violations in Zim.
metadata.Further information: Before the national shutdown, Zimbabwean civil servants rejected a 10% salary increase and planned to go on a strike in two weeks time. The strike will see 300 000 public workers take to the streets. The fuel price increase further aggravated workers and the rest of the country, which led to the shutdown before the planned strike. Human rights organisations have called for a stop to the human rights violations allegedly perpetrated by military police against civilians. The SA finance department has since said that it declined to give Zimbabwe a $1billion loan.
